catalog_quote: [Trager 1946 p.189, sec. 2:221] Stress is a phonemic feature of Taos, existing in the form of loud stress, medial stress, and weak stress. The first two may be combined with any one of the three tones. That stress as such is phonemic is indicated by the fact that no rules on a phonemic level can be devised determining the place of the stressed syllables in a word, and such rules as can be laid down for certain morphological combinations are either very complicated or show many exceptions. There are not many instances of words distinguished by the position of loud stress alone (that is, without accompanying tone differences), but there are some ... Moreover, many nouns vary the stress patterns as between singular and plural absolute forms, and these changes are as important to correct apprehension of the forms as those in the suffixes. ... Medial stress is found only where a loud stress …

tone_statements.citation: Sutton, Logan. 2014. Kiowa-Tanoan: A Synchronic and Diachronic Study. Ph.D. dissertation, University of New Mexico, Department of Linguistics (UNM Digital Repository, Linguistics ETDs 34). 1293 pp.
tone_statements.quote: As in the other branches of the family, the Tiwa languages do seem to have phonemic tone. Unfortunately, it is poorly described. George Trager analyzed Taos Tiwa has having three tone levels—high, mid, and low—and three stress levels—strong, medium, and weak. [...] However, Hull (1973) analyzes the language as having three tones just like Kiowa, Tewa, and Towa: high, falling, and low. Kontak and Kunkel (1987) follow suit in their work. A cursory examination of certain morphophonological features and of the Tiwa translation of the Book of Luke (which has tone marking) suggests that almost all words end up with a high or falling tone, indicating some kind of pitch accent system.
tone_statements.summary: Phonemic tone acknowledged but analysis unsettled: Trager's 3 level tones (H/M/L) x 3 stresses vs. Hull 1973 / Kontak & Kunkel 1987's 3 tones high/falling/low with independent stress; Sutton suspects a pitch accent-like system (words ending in H or falling).

tone_statements.citation: Trager, George L. 1944. Spanish and English Loanwords in Taos. International Journal of American Linguistics 10(4): 144-158.
tone_statements.quote: … and the accent-marks 'a, ,a, á, à. … The loud and medial stresses with middle (normal) tone, 'a and ,a, are much as the loud and reduced-loud of English ('trolley- ,car, ,good 'night); á is high tone (higher than normal), à is low tone (lower, and drawled), both high- and low-toned syllables having medial stress when there is a loud normal stress in the same word; weak syllables, unmarked, are short and slurred, with normal tone, except that final weak syllables two syllables after a loud stress are usually somewhat raised in pitch.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Three tones, middle (normal), high and low, marked on syllables together with three stress degrees (loud, medial, weak); weak syllables have normal tone; most Spanish loans keep the Spanish stress.

sources.note: The work describes the Santa Clara dialect of Tewa (Glottolog tewa1260), a different Kiowa-Tanoan language, not Taos or Northern Tiwa; its statements cannot be transferred to nort1550. Note also that the listed open_urlhttp://wals.info/refdb/record/360resolves to the WALS record Holmer-1949d (Goajiro phonology), a wrong record; the correct WALS record is Hoijer-and-Dozier-1949, and the article itself was read from the public archive.org copy of IJAL 15(3).
